title.en: Dan Kun the Sandal Prince of the Ever-White Mountains

texts.period: Corean traditional history recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882; rev. ed.); episode dated c. 2356 BC

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In this variant of the founding, of old the land had neither prince nor chiefs. A Divine Being descended from heaven and took up his abode at the foot of a sandalwood tree on the Ever-White Mountains. The people of the land became his subjects, made him sovereign, and called him Dan Kun, the Sandal Prince, and his realm Cho-sen, Morning Calm. His descendants reigned more than a thousand years, until the occupation of the country by the Chinese noble Ki Tsze.
summary.zh: 古時朝鮮無君無長。有神人自天而降，止於白山檀樹之下。土人尊之為君，號曰檀君，其國曰朝鮮（晨靜之國）。子孫相承千餘年，至中國貴人箕子東來而代興。

sensitivity.note: Nineteenth-century Western compilation of the Dangun tradition; variant form of the same founding story as records 'dangun' and 'korean-dangun-wanggeom'.

passages.text: According to Corean tradition, of old the land had neither prince nor chiefs. A Divine Being descended from heaven and took up his abode at the foot of a sandalwood tree on the Ever-White Mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The people of the land became his subjects, made him their sovereign, and called him Dan Kun, the Sandal Prince, and his realm Cho-sen, Morning Calm. This took place in the time of Tang Ti Yao, in 2356 BC.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His first residence was at Ping-an; later he transferred it to Pe-yo, where his descendants remained till the eighth year of the emperor Wu Ting, when they were established in Mount Asstak. His descendants reigned in Cho-sen more than one thousand years, and then followed the occupation of the country by the Chinese noble Ki Tsze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Born of the Gourd-Egg: The Shinra Founding Variant

texts.period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the local legends of Shinra, after the invasion of Cho-sen many of the original inhabitants fled and scattered over the east coast. The head man of a village, hearing the neighing of horses toward a mountain, finds not a horse but an egg of extraordinary size shaped like a gourd; breaking it open he discovers a beautiful rosy boy-baby, adopts him, and when the boy is thirteen the elders of the six principal towns choose him as their lord. The country is named Born of the Gourd-Egg, and the new king takes to wife a fair maiden reputed the offspring of a well-dragon; they reign sixty years, when their daughter succeeds to the throne.
summary.zh: 新羅別傳云：古朝鮮被侵，遺民散居嶺東。一村長聞山間馬嘶而往視，非馬也，乃大卵一枚，形如瓠。剖之，得赤色俊兒，養為己子。兒年十三，六部酋長共立為主。名其國曰瓠卵所生，王娶井龍之女為后，在位六十年，女繼其統。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Hyokkose birth legend (cf. korean-hyeokgeose-luminous-egg); Western compilation of local tradition.

passages.text: The mythical origin and founding of Shinra is thus told in the local legends of the place. After the invasion of Cho-sen by the Chinese emperor, many of the original inhabitants fled and scattered over the east coast, making settlements on the mountains, in the valleys, and along the sea-shore, some of which grew to be cities and large towns.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the attention of the head man of one of the villages was attracted by the neighing of horses toward a mountain. He went in the direction of the sounds, but instead of a horse he found an egg of extraordinary size, shaped like a gourd. Carefully breaking it open, he discovered a beautiful rosy boy-baby inside. The old man's heart was touched, and he took the child home and adopted it as his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy grew up beloved of all. When but thirteen years old, the elders of the six principal towns gathered together and chose him as their lord and master. They gave him a name signifying Coming Out of the West, and to the country a name meaning Born of the Gourd-egg. The new king took to wife a fair maiden reputed to be the offspring of a well-dragon. They reigned for sixty years, when their daughter succeeded to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Opened in Presence of the Crows

texts.period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the fifth year of the daughter-queen's reign she marries a youth from afar whose origin is as wonderful as her parents'. His mother the queen had been delivered of an egg; her husband threw it away, but the queen wrapped it in a silk napkin with other treasures, set it adrift on the sea, and after many days it washed ashore. Fishermen netted it and threw it back into the sea; it drifted into a harbor of Shinra, where an old woman opened the lid and found a lovely boy with a smile on his face. Crows stood around the shore at his finding, and the crone named him Opened in Presence of the Crows. He grew nine feet high, excelled in geomancy, built himself a house on a lucky site, and the queen married him to her daughter.
summary.zh: 女主五年，嫁遠來奇男子。其母亦係產卵者：夫棄卵，后以繒裹之，雜寶物納櫝浮海。久之漂至新羅港，漁者網得復投海，旋為老嫗所拾，啟櫝見兒，笑靨嫣然。時羣鴉集岸，嫗因名之曰『烏前開者』。兒長九尺，精堪輿，自擇吉地而居。女王遂以女妻之。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Seok Talhae drift-egg legend (cf. korean-seoktalhae-egg-across-sea); Western compilation.

passages.text: In the fifth year of her reign she married a youth who had come from afar, whose origin was as wonderful as that of her own parents. His mother the queen had been delivered of an egg. Her husband, not enjoying such a form of offspring, threw the egg away, but the queen recovering it, carefully wrapped it in a silk napkin, and with many other treasures put it in a box and set it adrift on the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: After many days the box was washed ashore on a distant coast. The fishermen who picked it up in their nets thought nothing of it, and threw it into the sea again. It drifted into one of the harbors of Shinra. An old woman finding it, opened the lid and found a lovely boy with a smile on his face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the old woman first picked up the waif, there were a number of crows standing around the shore, and the crone gave him a name referring to the presence of these birds — Opened in Presence of the Crows. He grew up a man of strength, nine feet high, excelling all other youths in bodily vigor. Excelling in the knowledge of geomancy, he found a good place for a residence and built on it. Hearing of his renown, the queen of Shinra married him to her daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Boy from the Grove where the Cock Crowed

texts.period: Local legend recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated legendary Silla antiquity

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: One evening the newly made king hears a cock crow in the woods toward the west. His servants find a small golden casket suspended from a tree with a white cock crowing beneath it; opened, the casket contains a boy baby, named The Golden Boy from the Grove in which the Cock Crowed. The boy grows up and succeeds his father; in the reign of the twenty-second king the people change the name of their country, Shin-han, to Shinra.
summary.zh: 新王一夜聞西林雞鳴，遣僕往探，見樹懸金櫝，下有白雞而鳴。取櫝啟之，中得一兒，名曰『雞鳴林中金童』。兒長而嗣父位。傳至二十二王，國人改新韓之名為新羅。

sensitivity.note: Variant of the Kim Alji / hen-casket legend (cf. korean-keumyunji-hen-woods-renaming); Western compilation.

passages.text: One evening the newly made king heard a cock crow in the woods toward the west. He sent his servants after it, who found a small golden casket suspended from a tree. Under it a white cock was crowing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The servant reported the matter to his master. Another servant was despatched to the place. He returned with the box, which, being opened, was found to contain a boy baby, who was given the name signifying The Golden Boy from the Grove in which the Cock crowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The baby boy grew up and succeeded his father. In the reign of the twenty-second king of the line, the people of the country, then called Shin-han, changed the name of their country to Shinra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Dragon-Kings of the Seas

region.en: Palaces under the four seas (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The riong, or dragon, chief of scaly monsters, embodies all the forces of motion and change. It possesses the gift of transformation, rendering itself visible or invisible at will; in spring it ascends to the skies and in autumn buries itself in the watery depths; it can shrink to the size of a silkworm or swell till it fills the space of heaven and earth. Celestial dragons guard the mansions of the gods so they do not fall; spiritual dragons make wind and rain for mankind; terrestrial dragons mark the courses of rivers; and another watches over hidden treasures — the dragon of mines and gems whom mortals must propitiate to win the metals. There are four dragon-kings with palaces under the northern, eastern, southern and western seas, whose terrible minister-dragons, battling in air and deep, cause the commotion of the elements; and the dragon carries on its forehead a pear-shaped pearl of wondrous healing and power. So intense is this belief that the mines of Cho-sen are little worked.
summary.zh: 龍者鱗蟲之長，具變化之能：可隱可現，春升秋潛，小如蠶而大則充塞天地。天龍守神宮使不傾，神龍興雲雨以利民，地龍畫江河之流，復有守寶之龍司礦藏——故朝鮮礦山多不開採，懼觸龍怒也。四海有龍王各居其宮，其屬龍相鬥於空中深海，遂起風雷。龍額有珠，療疾增力，得之者勝。

sensitivity.note: Sino-Korean dragon cosmology compiled by a Western observer; shared East Asian heritage rather than uniquely Korean.

passages.text: The riong, or dragon, whose figure as depicted in Corean art is perhaps nothing more than a highly idealized form of an extinct geological species of saurian, is one of the four supernatural creatures. He is an embodiment of all the forces of motion, change, and power in animal life, with the mysterious attributes of the serpent. It possesses the gift of transformation and of rendering itself visible or invisible at will; in the spring it ascends to the skies and in the autumn buries itself in the watery depths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: This omnipotent monster becomes at will reduced to the size of a silkworm or swollen till it fills the space of heaven and earth. It desires to mount, and it rises until it affronts the clouds; to sink, and it descends until hidden below the fountains of the deep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The functions of the celestial dragon are to guard the mansions of the gods in heaven so that they do not fall; of the spiritual, to cause the wind to blow and produce rain for the benefit of mankind; of the terrestrial, to mark out the courses of rivers and streams; while another watches over the hidden treasures concealed from mortals. This last is the dragon that presides over mines and gems, and which mortals must propitiate or overcome in order to gain the precious metals out of the earth. Intense belief in the dragon is one of the chief reasons why the mines in Cho-sen are so little worked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are four dragon-kings who have their palaces in the world under the sea, one ruling in the northern, one in the eastern, one in the southern, and one in the western sea. The ministers and messengers of these four monarchs are the terrible dragons whose battles in the air and in the deep are the causes of the commotion of the elements. In common belief the dragon carries on his forehead a pear-shaped pearl, supposed to possess wondrous virtues of healing and power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Guardian Serpent of the Household

texts.period: Ethnographic observation recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: In the peninsula not only are trees reverenced as the abode of spirits, but the sa, or snakes, are rarely if ever harmed. The people feed, venerate and even worship them as the guardian genii of their households; the epkurong-gi is the name they call the serpent which presides over their family Edens. Instead of being looked on as the embodiment of evil as in Semitic lore, the serpent's presence is hailed as an omen of blessing. A serpent that lives a thousand years bears in its head a glistening gem called ya-kang-chiu; the guardian serpent is pictured as double-winged, with forked tongue, flying among the clouds and protecting its worshippers by pursuing their enemies — as on the war-flags the Corean mountaineers carried to the Han River forts in 1871.
summary.zh: 朝鮮人敬樹為神棲之所，而於蛇尤不敢害。飼之、敬之、甚至奉之為家宅守護之神，名曰埃闊龍基（家蛇）。蛇至千年，首生寶珠，名牙剛珠（如鑽石）。守蛇之神有雙翼、吐信，飛行雲間，逐敵護主——同治十年（1871）漢江要塞獵虎軍之戰旗，即繪此蛇神。

sensitivity.note: Household serpent cult recorded ethnographically; no living-community restriction on describing historical belief.

passages.text: In the peninsula not only are trees reverenced as the abode of spirits, but the sa, or snakes, are rarely, if ever, harmed. The people feed, venerate, and even worship them as the guardian genii of their households. The epkurong-gi is the name by which they call the serpent which presides over their family Edens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Instead of being looked upon as the embodiment of the principle of evil, as in Semitic lore, their presence is hailed as an omen of blessing. They are treated like pets. In their heads they are believed to carry a precious jewel after they have lived long. A serpent often lives to be one thousand years old, and then bears in his front a glistening gem, called ya-kang-chiu, a name the people also apply to any glittering stone, especially the diamond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The guardian serpent is represented as double-winged, with forked tongue, flying among the clouds and protecting its worshippers by pursuing their enemies. The illustration here given is copied from one of the war-flags carried by the Corean mountaineers from their homes to the forts on the Han River in 1871.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kirin and the Phoenix as Omens of Good Rule

texts.period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The kirin, with the body of a deer and the tail of an ox and a single soft horn, never treads on or injures any living being. It is the emblem of perfect rectitude and the incarnate essence of the five primordial elements; its appearance on earth is ever a happy omen, the harbinger of good government and the birth of good rulers. The phoenix likewise appears at or near the birth of a good ruler; in its plumage the sheen of five colors typifies the five cardinal virtues, and it is the emblem not only of auspicious government but of inseparable fellowship and conjugal love.
summary.zh: 麒麟鹿身牛尾，額有軟角，不履生草，不傷生靈，為至德之瑞、五行之精。其現世則善政將興、明君將生。鳳凰亦然：五色文采應五常之德，見則天下太平，且象夫婦和鳴之義。

sensitivity.note: Shared East Asian auspicious-beast lore compiled by a Western observer.

passages.text: The kirin is another of the four supernatural creatures, depicted in Corean art especially as a symbol of peace and joy. This beast has the body of a deer and the tail of an ox, and on its forehead a single soft horn. It is said never to tread on or injure any living being. It is the emblem of perfect rectitude, and the incarnate essence of the five primordial elements of all things: water, fire, wood, metal, earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Its appearance on the earth is ever regarded as a happy omen, as the harbinger of good government and the birth of good rulers. The male beast is called ki and the female rin or lin; the two words combined form the general term kirin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The phoenix, like the kirin, appears on the earth at or near the birth of a good ruler, and hence is the emblem of peace and good government. In its marvellous plumage the sheen of the five colors may be descried, each of which is typical of the five cardinal virtues. It is not only a symbol of auspicious government, but of inseparable fellowship, and many stanzas of poetry refer to it as typical of courtship and conjugal love.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Divine Tortoise of the Yellow River

texts.period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The tortoise is the center of a great circle of superstitions. In Chinese legend a divine tortoise emerged from the Yellow River, on the shell of which a sage discovered the system of numerals and thus the foundation of mathematics and the rudiments of philosophy. This tortoise was the embodiment of the star in Ursa Major and progenitor of the tortoise tribe; it can transform itself into other forms of life and lives to ten thousand years, the symbol of long life. Ten kinds of tortoises exist, one half dragon with a tail like a fringe of silver — attendant of the god of waters, and so used as the top of a well. Many Corean gateways are surmounted with huge stone tortoises; the great seal of state, the regalia of sovereignty in Cho-sen, has the form of a tortoise; and the huge tortoise that supports mountains on its back has a shell a thousand leagues in circumference.
summary.zh: 龜負河圖而出，聖人得數理之原，遂開數學與哲學之端。此龜乃北斗之星精所化，龜族之祖；能變形他類，壽萬歲，故為長壽之符。龜有十種，其一半龍半龜，尾如銀纓，為水神之侍，故井欄多飾龜形。城門石龜、御寶龍龜，皆以鎮固之意；至若馱山巨龜，甲周一千里，則天地之支柱也。

sensitivity.note: Sino-Korean tortoise symbolism compiled by a Western observer.

passages.text: The tortoise is the centre of a great circle of pleasing superstitions, and hence is one of the set of symbols oftenest employed in Corean art. The practice of divination is mostly associated with tortoise-shell, the figuring of a tortoise's back having a mystic signification.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Chinese legend a divine tortoise emerged from the Yellow River, on the shell of which a sage discovered the system of numerals, and thus obtained the foundation of mathematics and the rudiments of philosophy. This tortoise was said to be the embodiment of the star in Ursa Major, and the progenitor of all the tortoise tribe. It can transform itself into other forms of life and lives to the age of ten thousand years. Hence it is the symbol of long life. It is said to conceive by thought alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are said to be ten kinds of tortoises, one of them being half dragon, half tortoise, with a tail like a fringe of silver. This is the attendant of the god of waters, and hence is often used as the top of a well. Many Corean gateways are surmounted with huge tortoises sculptured in stone. The great seal of state, the regalia of sovereignty in Cho-sen, has the form of a tortoise. A common idea in Cho-sen, as in China, is the huge tortoise which supports mountains on its back, and having a shell which is one thousand leagues in circumference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fish-Man of the Eastern Sea

texts.period: Mythical zoology recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The in-e, fish-man or merman, is a sort of siren supposed to inhabit the Sea of Japan and the Eastern Sea. It is six or seven feet long, and in head and body resembles a human being, its nose, mouth, ears and arms or flippers covered with white skin without scales; it has a long slender tail like a horse's. It suckles its young and sheds tears when its offspring are captured — and perhaps this is the creature around Quelpart whose tears produce pearls.
summary.zh: 東海有人魚，長六七尺，首身似人，鼻口耳臂皆有白膚無鱗，尾細長如馬尾。能哺乳其子，子為人所獲則泣。或謂濟州海中亦有其類，其淚化為珠。

passages.text: The in-e, fish-man or merman, is a sort of siren that is supposed to inhabit the Sea of Japan and the Eastern Sea, but whether partly fabulous or entirely real, we are unable to say. It is six or seven feet long, and in its head and body resembles a human being, as its nose, mouth, ears, and arms, or flippers, are covered with white skin without scales. It has a long and slender tail, like that of a horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: It suckles its young, and sheds tears when its offspring are captured. It is probable that this creature is the same as a reported dog-fish or shark living in the seas around Quelpart, whose tears produce pearls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Dragons' Teeth: The Drought Riot of 1882

texts.period: Contemporary event interpreted by folk belief, recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); episode dated July 1882

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 33, eBook #67141

summary.en: The people believe that all the forces of nature are under the control of spirits, who will give or withhold sunshine or rain, send blasting mildew and pestilence, or fertility, plenty and joy, according as they are pleased or displeased. On this soil a demagogue may sow dragons' teeth: in the long drought that ruined the rice crop of 1882, the leaders of the anti-foreign faction persuaded the common people that the spirits were annoyed at the introduction of foreigners and therefore withheld the rain. This belief was strengthened when it rained heavily for many hours after the Japanese had been driven out of Seoul in the frightful massacre of the ministers.
summary.zh: 朝鮮人信天地風雨皆聽於神，神喜怒則雨暘疫豐隨之。故煽惑者可播『龍牙』而亂起。光緒八年（1882）大旱米貴，排外黨魁乃倡言：神怒西人入境，故不降雨。及壬午兵變殺日本使館人後，大雨連時，眾信愈堅，以為神鑒其誅而降澤。

sensitivity.note: Historical riot interpreted through folk belief; mentions real violence (1882 Imo mutiny) in summary terms only.

passages.text: They believe that all these creatures and all the forces of nature are under the control of the spirits, who will give or withhold sunshine or rain, send blasting mildew and pestilence, or fertility, plenty and joy, according as they are pleased or displeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: It will be seen at once what a soil the demagogue has for sowing dragons' teeth, and what frightful popular commotion may be stirred up by playing upon the fears of the populace. The most recent illustration of this is seen in the frightful massacre of the ministers and the Japanese, in July 1882.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The long drought having ruined the rice crop, the leaders of the anti-foreign faction persuaded the common people that the spirits were annoyed at the introduction of foreigners, and therefore withheld the rain. In this belief they were strengthened from the fact that it rained heavily for many hours after the Japanese had been driven out of Seoul.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 33 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Wishes and the Pudding on the Nose

texts.period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: Two poor old married folk lament the winter, pray to Heaven, and an angel grants them three things and no more. They cannot decide between riches, health, long life and a child — until at bedtime the old woman wishes for three feet of pudding to toast on the brazier, which appears at once. The enraged husband wishes it to hang from her nose; it does. He laments losing a wish; she tries to hang herself; and finally she spends the last wish on getting the pudding off. A voice from heaven rebukes their vain desires; they eat the pudding, adopt an orphan, and from that night abstain from foolish wishes.
summary.zh: 貧夫婦寒夜相對歎貧，禱於天。天使忽降，賜三願。議之未決，嫗臨睡忽曰：『若有三尺餅炙於爐，豈不美哉！』言未畢，餅已置於側。翁怒罵：『願此餅黏於汝鼻！』餅即飛黏嫗鼻。嫗欲自縊，翁懼而止之，許以末願取下。嫗曰：『願餅落。』言訖餅墜地，天上有聲責其妄願。二人啖餅，養孤兒為嗣，自是不復妄求。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale from missionary-collected material; the ATU 'three wishes' type in a Korean telling.

passages.text: There were once two old married folks who had not a single child. Extremely poor, they lived a pitiable life. One cold winter evening, after supper, they gazed into the fire in the brazier and lamented that for the poor, winter is a rough time, with neither food for the mouth nor fuel; if they go out over the mountain through rain or snow to seek wood, they die of cold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: They prayed fervently to the Deity, when suddenly an angel appeared: 'In spite of your sin of murmuring, Heaven having pitied you, accords you three things, after which you can ask no more. Reflect well, choose, and ask.' They could not decide: riches, freedom from sickness, long life, or a child? At the moment of lying down to sleep, the old woman, stirring the fire with the tongs, reflected, 'If we could have three or four feet of pudding to set to toast on this brazier, that would be royally excellent.' She spoke, and there was three feet of food placed by her side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The husband, beside himself with rage, screamed out, 'Oh, what a woman! To punish you I wish the pudding would hang itself on the point of your nose.' Immediately the pudding made a leap and attached itself to the old dame's nose. He cried that he too had lost a wish; the woman in tears took a cord to strangle herself; and the husband, touched with compassion, said, 'Stop, there remains one wish to us. Have your own way about it.' 'If that is so, I wish that what hangs to my nose comes loose.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: She had hardly finished speaking when the sausage fell plump to the ground, and out of the midst of heaven an angry voice was heard: 'You have obtained the three things you wished for, and have you gained a great advantage? If you wish to enjoy true blessing, be content to live with what Heaven gives, and do not form vain desires.' The two old folks ate the pudding, and on the morrow, agreeably to their supreme ambition of having a baby, adopted a little fatherless and motherless orphan, and lived happily to extreme old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

region.zh: 全羅道邑城（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: A politician in the chief city of Chulla owes the government ten thousand strings of cash and awaits execution. He cajoles the jailer into letting him out at night, then persuades the governor that a dead debtor is worth nothing alive, and secures a stay — visiting nightly. On his rounds he has a sketch of a human nose sealed by the governor, then travels the coast with three accomplices telling a rich doctor's son that the king is sick and can be cured only by a medicine concocted from a nose exactly like the sketch, which matches his father's. The son buys off the 'royal messengers' at vast cost, and dares tell no one until his father's death: 'I have bought my father's nose for ten thousand strings of cash.'
summary.zh: 全羅道邑有政客負官帑萬緡，論死。賂獄卒夜縱之，說太守曰：『殺我則帑無著，生我則帑可還。』得緩刑。又請太守於人鼻畫上用印，乃攜黨徒沿海行詐：詭言王疾，非得與畫同之鼻入藥不瘳，而某富翁之父之鼻恰合。其子懼，出巨金贖之。父死乃自言：『吾以萬緡買父之鼻也。』

sensitivity.note: Folk satire on officialdom; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the chief city of Chulla there was a politician who was in debt to the government to the amount of ten thousand strings of cash. Unable to pay, he was condemned to death. Bethinking himself of a stratagem, he so besought the jailer that, struck with compassion, the man let him go free for a while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight he presented himself before the door where the governor slept, and argued: 'If you put your servant to death this will be simply one man of means less in the world, and the money I owe will be lost to the government. If, on the contrary, you preserve my life, I shall repay the whole of my debt.' He visited again the next night, drew from his sleeve a sketch representing a human nose, and besought the governor to put his seal upon it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He now associated three companions, and on the coast of the Eastern Sea they found the grand mansion of a rich noble. Taking the son aside, the officer declared: 'The king is very sick, and all the physicians have declared that the only means of healing is to find the nose of a man just like this and to concoct a remedy from it. We have been commanded, without distinction of place or person, to strike off such a nose and produce it at Court. Your honorable father's nose exactly resembles this.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son cried out that cutting off his old father's nose was impossible, and the officer replied: 'As this is a matter of a son devoted to his father, we shall not cut off the nose; but if you will give us a certain sum we will go elsewhere to procure a nose which we shall present to the king.' He accepted a sum equal to many times ten thousand strings of cash, and warned the son to say nothing. Overjoyed at not having his parent's nose amputated, the son dared let no one know until the day of his father's death; then breaking the silence he said, 'I have bought my father's nose for ten thousand strings of cash.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: King Cheng-chong and the Examination in the Night

region.en: Streets and examination hall, Seoul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 漢城市廛試院（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Korean royal anecdote recorded by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); King Chongjo reigned 1776-1800

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: King Cheng-chong, celebrated for goodness, goes out one night disguised as a countryman. Peeping through a hole in the paper door of a miserable house he sees an old man weeping, a man in mourning singing, and a nun dancing. Questioned, the man in mourning explains: his wife has cut and sold her last hair to buy bean-soup for his starving old father, becoming bareheaded like a nun; the old man weeps at degrading her; and to console him, wife and husband dance and sing. The king, moved, invents an examination for the morrow with the subject 'the song of a man in mourning, the dance of a nun, the tears of an old man'; no student can fathom it, but the poor householder alone knows it perfectly, wins the doctorate, and is loaded with office for his filial piety.
summary.zh: 正祖微行夜出，穴紙窺一貧家：見老翁泣、居喪者歌、尼而舞者三人。詰之，其人曰：『家貧無以養親，妻剪盡髮鬻之市豆羹以奉舅姑，遂如尼。舅愧而泣，妻舞以解之，我亦歌。』王大異之，翌日突設科試，題即『喪者之歌、尼之舞、老翁之淚』。諸生皆不解，惟此人切中，遂擢甲第，旌其孝。

passages.text: There was in Cho-sen a king called His Majesty Cheng-chong, celebrated in all the kingdom for his goodness. One night, disguised as a countryman and accompanied only by a single companion, he started out to make a circuit to inform himself of the temper of his subjects. Arrived at a certain point he looked in the window of a miserable house, punched a peep-hole in the paper door and perceived an old man weeping, a man in mourning singing, and a nun or widow dancing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Questioned, the man in mourning explained: 'In my hut one could never find sufficient grain for a meal. I have no victuals for my old father. Morning and evening, in default of all other resource, my wife has often cut off a tress of her hair and sold it to buy a cup of bean-soup, which she offers to my father. This evening she clipped and sold all the hair that remained, and has become bare-headed like a nun. My old father, seeing that for his sake his young daughter-in-law has become a nun, broke out weeping: why have I lived to degrade my daughter-in-law? To console him my wife danced, and I, although in mourning, joined in with song.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king was impressed with such marked devotion, and said, 'How will it do to present you at the examination to-morrow?' No examination was known; but no sooner did the great clock-bell vibrate than he ordered an examination published during the night, to the astonishment of the literary men. The subject was: 'The song of a man in mourning, the dance of a nun, the tears of an old man.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of all the students not one could derive the sense of such a subject; this man alone knew it perfectly well, because he had had experience of those very things in his own house. He treated the theme clearly, and the king, having examined the essay and found it without a mistake, gave the degree of doctor and loaded him with office, recompensing the filial piety of the son and daughter-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prodigious Effects of a Looking-Glass

region.zh: 慶尚道村邑（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Korean folk tale collected in the Grammaire Coreenne, retold by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882)

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 34, eBook #67141

summary.en: A young noble of Kiung-sang province journeys to Seoul, and his wife begs him to bring back the lovely glass-like thing of which she has heard: if you look in it you will see a very curious thing. He buys a mirror and packs it unexamined. At home the wife looks, sees a woman, and storms that he has brought home a concubine; he looks and sees a man, and cries that she keeps a libertine — the old mother looks and sees the widow Pak, the grandfather the fee-collecting teacher, and the whole village sees only itself. Finally the magistrate summons his men and horses to receive the new officer he supposes has displaced him — until a young policeman demonstrates how the glass reflects every face that gazes into it.
summary.zh: 慶尚士人將赴漢京，其妻囑購『照之則見奇物』之寶鏡。歸而妻照，見婦，怒詬夫攜妾；夫照，見男，斥妻藏漢；婆照，見白媼；翁照，見索脩之塾師；闔村競照，唯見己身，喧然告官。太守照之，見一官人，以為新官至而奪己位，亟備車馬。一少年捕快熟視，乃悟：鏡中所見，皆照者之面也。

sensitivity.note: Folk satire; city-folk tale about country bumpkins; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: A young noble of Kiung-sang province was going on a journey to Seoul. Just as he was about to depart, his wife called him: 'I have heard the mother of Mr. Kim speak of a very lovely thing which looks like glass and pretty metal. They say that if you look in it you will see a very curious thing. You must bring me one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having finished his business at Seoul he made the purchase of a mirror through one of his friends, and put his wife's commission in his wallet without even looking at it. When he arrived home, she hastened to take out the mirror. At once she perceived in it a woman, and began to weep and berate her husband for bringing along a concubine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The amazed husband looked in the mirror, and at the side of his wife perceived a man; he was about to murder his wife, when his old mother came in. Looking in the mirror she saw a woman and broke into a laugh: 'Is it because you see the old woman, your neighbor, that you dispute? The widow Pak has come to get some fire.' The venerable grandfather entered the children's room, perceived in the mirror an aged man, and grumbled that the puppy of the teacher Tsoi had come to collect his fees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The people of the village, one by one, two by two, all looked at the mirror and made a tumult. They carried it to the magistrate, who, more astonished than the others, ordered: 'A new officer has arrived, why have I lost my place? Get ready men and horses for him.' He believed he had been cashiered, until a young policeman, after careful examination of the mirror, pointed out the manner in which the visage of each individual was reflected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 34 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Winged Tiger of the War-Flags

texts.period: Ethnographic record by Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882); the banner described from the 1871 campaign

source.work: William Elliot Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation (1882), ch. 36, eBook #67141

summary.en: Both actually and ideally the tiger is the symbol of power and fierceness in Corea; popular superstition attributes to him the powers of flying, of emitting fire and hurling lightning. The flag of the tiger-hunters from the northern provinces who faced the marines in 1871 was a winged tiger rampant, spitting fire and holding the lightnings in his lifted fore-claws, embodying the powers of earth, air and heaven — the tutelary genius of the descendants of the aboriginal worshippers of the tiger. From the most ancient times the tiger has been an object of religious reverence; the cry of the name tu-e', the fabulous enemy of the tiger, acts as a charm against the man-eater.
summary.zh: 虎者朝鮮威猛之象。俗信其能飛、口吐火、爪掣雷。同治十年獵虎軍戰旗，繪有翼猛虎，口噴火，爪擎電，蓋天地人三才之力萃焉——此虎圖騰遺民之守護神也。虎自古被尊為神。又有神獸曰土嵬者為虎所懼，夜呼『土嵬』可退虎患。

sensitivity.note: Tiger cult recorded ethnographically; the 1871 conflict is referenced only as provenance of the banner.

passages.text: Both actually and ideally the tiger is the symbol of power and fierceness. The flag of the tiger-hunters, from the northern provinces of Ping-an or Ham-kiung, who bravely faced the rifles of the United States marines and sailors in 1871, was a winged tiger rampant, spitting fire, holding the lightnings in his lifted fore-claws, and thus embodying the powers of earth, air, and heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is the tutelary genius of the descendants of the aboriginal worshippers of the tiger, who even yet cling to the religion of the soil. Popular superstition attributes to him the powers of flying, of emitting fire and hurling lightning. From the most ancient times it has been an object of religious reverence: 'They also worshipped the tiger, which they looked on as a god,' was written of the people living on the sea of Japan before the Christian era.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: To drive away the dreaded kal-pem, the people invoke the aid of the tu-e, a fabulous monster, which is the enemy of the tiger, and which the latter greatly fears. The cry of his name, tu-e, tu-e, is believed to act as a charm, and is often raised by villagers at night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Griffis, Corea: The Hermit Nation, ch. 36 (1882); not verbatim.
